summary: This proof check names no overall winner. Established: S1 (Speaker 1) has shown that remote-by-default holds for focused solo work where fewer interruptions raise output, plus a workable hybrid qualification for juniors; S2 (Speaker 2) has shown a real unanswered cost in lost informal problem-solving and a genuine junior-onboarding objection that S1 concedes. Unshown: S1's broad productivity premise and S2's never-meet, companies, and motive attacks, which break.

points.title: S1 (Speaker 1) — Step 1: productivity premise (n2 -> n1): breaks
points.text: Depends on the definition of 'productive' as more output on focused tasks and the assumption that controlling one's environment raises measured output for software work. Step breaks: 'People are more productive when they control their environment' (n2) is broader than any evidence given -- no task or measure is stated -- so the move from n2 to 'Remote work should be the default for software teams' (n1) claims more than this step shows.

points.title: S1 (Speaker 1) — Step 2: fewer interruptions (n3 -> n1): holds
points.text: Depends on the definition of interruptions as office intrusions on focused tasks and the assumption that fewer interruptions convert to more output. Step holds: 'fewer interruptions means more output' (n3) is the transcript's own narrower claim about focused tasks, so n3 genuinely supports n1 for that class of work.

points.title: S1 (Speaker 1) — Step 3: junior concession (n9): holds
points.text: Depends on the assumption that juniors learn faster with in-person observation, granted from the other side's objection. Step holds: 'Maybe juniors need a hybrid period, then remote by default' (n9) follows honestly from granting the onboarding objection and narrows the thesis (n1) rather than abandoning it.

points.title: S2 (Speaker 2) — Step 1: informal conversations (n4 -> n1): holds as a challenge
points.text: Depends on the definition of real problem solving as including informal hallway talk and the assumption that remote teams cannot fully replace it. Step holds as an unanswered challenge: 'Teams lose the informal conversations where most real problem solving happens' (n4) names a genuine cost of n1 that S1 never rebuts, though it does not by itself refute the default.

points.title: S2 (Speaker 2) — Steps 2-4: never-meet, companies, motive (n5, n6, n7): break
points.text: Depend on the assumption that the other side's thesis is read at its strongest. Each step breaks: 'people should never meet and just sit alone forever' (n5) misrepresents the 'default' of n1 as an only option; 'every successful company I know brings people back to the office' (n6) generalizes from a handful of companies to all; 'You only say this because you hate commuting' (n7) attacks motive instead of argument. None of these refutes n1.

points.title: S2 (Speaker 2) — Step 5: junior onboarding (n8): holds
points.text: Depends on the definition of onboarding speed as time for a junior to learn by watching seniors and the assumption that observation needs proximity. Step holds: 'onboarding a junior developer remotely is clearly slower' (n8) is the one S2 attack S1 grants in n9, so it stands as shown on the transcript's own terms.
